title: The Slowest Worker Sets the Pace

scenes.visual: Title card 'The Slowest Worker Sets the Pace' over a cup of leaf disks under a desk lamp. Same colour map as the first film: carbon dioxide = BLUE, water = TEAL, light = YELLOW, glucose = AMBER, oxygen gas = RED. A RATE METER (dial labelled 'relative net oxygen build-up (flotation proxy)', no units or numbers) sits in the top-right corner for the whole film; it stands for faster or slower net oxygen build-up in matched disks, not a measured oxygen-per-minute reading. Molecules are labelled blocks and cartoons, never chemical structures; numbers only as on-screen text; anything not computed is labelled 'schematic'. Cream background, 16:9.

scenes.tts: The first film showed what a plant builds its sugar from. This film asks how fast it can build. Why does more light stop speeding a leaf up?
scenes.visual: A quick recap strip slides by: BLUE carbon dioxide and TEAL water blocks becoming an AMBER glucose block, with a YELLOW ray, then the strip shrinks to an icon. A YELLOW lamp brightens over a leaf; the RATE METER needle climbs, then stops and twitches. A question mark appears over the stuck needle.
scenes.narration: The first film showed what a plant builds its sugar from. This film asks how fast it can build. Why does more light stop speeding a leaf up?

scenes.tts: Here is a way to watch the rate. Punch small disks out of a spinach leaf. Pull the air out of them so they sink. Drop them into water with baking soda.
scenes.visual: Cartoon hand with a straw punches ten green disks from a spinach leaf. A syringe pulls air out (tiny bubbles leave the disks). The disks drop into a clear cup and sink to the bottom. A spoon of white powder labelled 'baking soda' goes in, and BLUE dots spread through the water.
scenes.narration: Here is a way to watch the rate. Punch small disks out of a spinach leaf. Pull the air out of them so they sink. Drop them into water with baking soda.

scenes.tts: Baking soda adds dissolved carbon dioxide. Now shine a lamp on the cup. As the disks photosynthesize, oxygen gas collects inside them. One by one, they float back up.
scenes.visual: Label on the BLUE dots: 'dissolved carbon dioxide'. A lamp switches on; YELLOW rays fall into the cup. Small RED bubbles form inside each disk, and the disks rise one at a time; a counter 'floating: 1 of 10 ... 10 of 10' ticks. The RATE METER needle rises as they float.
scenes.narration: Baking soda adds dissolved carbon dioxide. Now shine a lamp on the cup. As the disks photosynthesize, oxygen gas collects inside them. One by one, they float back up.

scenes.tts: The sooner they float, the faster the rate. Move the lamp closer, step by step. Each time, the disks float sooner. Plot the rate against brightness, and the curve climbs.
scenes.visual: A graph builds at right: x-axis 'light (lamp closer →)', y-axis 'rate'. The lamp steps closer in four jumps; at each jump the disks reset, float faster, and a new point drops on the graph. Points join into a rising line (computed from rate = smaller of a light-limited rate and a carbon dioxide cap; label 'computed, relative units'). Caption tag on the rising line: 'light is holding the rate back'.
scenes.narration: The sooner they float, the faster the rate. Move the lamp closer, step by step. Each time, the disks float sooner. Plot the rate against brightness, and the curve climbs.

scenes.tts: This cup has only a pinch of baking soda. Keep moving the lamp closer. Does the curve keep climbing? Make your guess.
scenes.visual: Inset: a pinch of white powder; only a few BLUE dots in the cup. The lamp hovers, ready to move closer. The graph's x-axis extends to the right with a dashed empty region labelled '?'.
scenes.narration: This cup has only a pinch of baking soda. Keep moving the lamp closer. Does the curve keep climbing? Make your guess.

scenes.visual: The lamp holds still; a 5-second countdown ring fills. The dashed '?' region of the graph pulses.

scenes.tts: It flattens. Brighter light now changes almost nothing. The disks are running short of carbon dioxide to build with. Carbon dioxide has become the slow worker, and the whole process waits for it.
scenes.visual: The lamp moves closer twice more; new points land at the same height and the line goes flat (computed). In the cup, the BLUE dots thin out and a small BLUE gauge labelled 'carbon dioxide supply' drops to low. A cartoon worker labelled 'carbon dioxide' stands at the flat part of the curve holding up a queue of YELLOW light packets. The RATE METER needle stays put.
scenes.narration: It flattens. Brighter light now changes almost nothing. The disks are running short of carbon dioxide to build with. Carbon dioxide has become the slow worker, and the whole process waits for it.

scenes.tts: An input or condition that holds a process back is called a limiting factor. On the rising part of this curve, it was light. On the flat part, it is carbon dioxide.
scenes.visual: Definition card: 'limiting factor = the input or condition that holds a process back'. The curve's rising part glows YELLOW with tag 'limit: light'; the flat part glows BLUE with tag 'limit: carbon dioxide'.
scenes.narration: An input or condition that holds a process back is called a limiting factor. On the rising part of this curve, it was light. On the flat part, it is carbon dioxide.

scenes.tts: So add more baking soda. Now the curve climbs higher before it flattens again. Something else, such as temperature or enzyme speed, now sets a new ceiling. When a curve is flat, more of that factor barely changes the rate.
scenes.visual: A big spoon of baking soda; the cup fills with BLUE dots and the gauge rises. A second computed curve draws above the first, rising further before levelling at a higher plateau (labelled 'more baking soda'). The first curve stays faint for comparison. A small tag at the new plateau: 'something else, such as temperature, sets this ceiling'. The lamp bumps closer on the flat part; the meter does not move.
scenes.narration: So add more baking soda. Now the curve climbs higher before it flattens again. Something else, such as temperature or enzyme speed, now sets a new ceiling. When a curve is flat, more of that factor barely changes the rate.

scenes.tts: Now leave the lab for the Chesapeake Bay. Underwater grasses grow on the bottom of its shallow water. Most eelgrass lives in the lower Bay, where the water is saltier.
scenes.visual: Map outline of the Chesapeake Bay (labelled 'schematic map'); the lower Bay is shaded and labelled 'saltier water'. Dive under the surface to a bed of green ribbon-like eelgrass on the bottom, swaying.
scenes.narration: Now leave the lab for the Chesapeake Bay. Underwater grasses grow on the bottom of its shallow water. Most eelgrass lives in the lower Bay, where the water is saltier.

scenes.tts: Light has to pass down through the water to reach the grass. Mud and floating algae block it. So does material growing on the leaves themselves.
scenes.visual: Side view of the water column. YELLOW rays enter at the surface and fade with depth (shading labelled 'schematic'). Brown mud particles, green floating algae dots, and a fuzzy coat on the eelgrass blades appear one by one as each is named, each dimming the YELLOW further.
scenes.narration: Light has to pass down through the water to reach the grass. Mud and floating algae block it. So does material growing on the leaves themselves.

scenes.tts: For the saltier Bay, there is a habitat target. More than twenty-two percent of the light at the surface should reach the grass. When murky water cuts the light, light can become the limiting factor.
scenes.caption: For the saltier Bay, there is a habitat target. More than 22 percent of the light at the surface should reach the grass. When murky water cuts the light, light can become the limiting factor.
scenes.visual: A horizontal dashed line across the water column labelled 'target: more than 22% of surface light reaches the grass'. In clear water the YELLOW reaches the bed above the line. The water clouds over; the YELLOW at the bed drops below the line, the eelgrass dims, and the RATE METER needle falls. Tag: 'limit: light'. A tiny inset of the first rate curve highlights its low, rising part.
scenes.narration: For the saltier Bay, there is a habitat target. More than 22 percent of the light at the surface should reach the grass. When murky water cuts the light, light can become the limiting factor.

scenes.tts: In this cup, with the other conditions held fixed, carbon dioxide capped the rate. In the Bay, murky water can make light the limit. Real plants can face two limits at once. A flat curve means more of that factor is no longer helping much.
scenes.visual: Split screen: the leaf-disk cup with the BLUE gauge low (tag 'cup: other conditions held fixed'), and the eelgrass bed with the YELLOW low (tag 'bay: light can limit'). In the cup, a hand moves the lamp closer on the flat part and the RATE METER does not move; then more baking soda is added and the meter climbs. A small tag between the panels: 'two factors can limit at once'.
scenes.narration: In this cup, with the other conditions held fixed, carbon dioxide capped the rate. In the Bay, murky water can make light the limit. Real plants can face two limits at once. A flat curve means more of that factor is no longer helping much.

scenes.visual: Hex end card. Take-home line on screen: 'One or more limiting factors cap how fast photosynthesis runs.'
